desc:
In one operation you may add 1 to any single element of nums. You may perform at most k operations (the same element may be chosen again and again).

The median of an array of length n is the element at zero-based position n // 2 after sorting (so for an even length it is the larger of the two middle values). Return the largest median you can reach.

nums = [2, 9, 4, 7], k = 5
sorted [2, 4, 7, 9], median = 7
add 3 to 7 and 1 to 9 -> [2, 4, 10, 10], median 10
answer = 10
hints: Raising anything below the median position is useless. Which elements decide the median?
To get a median of at least m, the upper half of the sorted array (from position n // 2 on) must consist of values at least m. What is the cheapest way to achieve that?
The cost of reaching median m is the sum of max(0, m - x) over the upper half, and it grows with m, so binary search the largest affordable m.
editorial: Sort the array. The median is the smallest element of the upper half a[n//2:]. For the median to be at least m, all n - n//2 elements of that half must be at least m, and it never helps to touch elements outside the half: raising the largest candidates is always cheapest, and those are exactly the upper-half elements.
So cost(m) = sum(max(0, m - x) for x in upper half). It is non-decreasing in m, so binary search the largest m between the current median and the current median plus k with cost(m) ≤ k.

Sorting is O(n log n) and the binary search adds O(n log k). A direct linear-after-sort water-filling approach (raise the smallest of the upper half until it meets the next one, and so on) gives the same result.
time: O(n log n + n log k)
